extracted.intended_audience: Coq developers, proof engineering researchers, and ML-for-code researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Learning and evaluating language-model-based formatting for Coq proof scripts: predicting spacing/linebreak/indentation between lexer tokens and integrating suggestions into Coq development workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task definition: spacing prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Task: predict spacing between tokens obtained from Coq’s lexer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain tokens and spacing via SerAPI’s sertok program; the model's output is a suggestion for spacing between two given Coq tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature representation for tokens and spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent tokenized sentences as S-expressions and represent spacing examples as tuples: (Content, Kind, #Newlines, #Spaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example sentence encoding: Sentence((IDENT Lemma)(IDENT mg_eq_proof)... (KEYWORD .))). Spacing example entries: [(null, BOS, 0, 0), (Lemma, IDENT, 2, 0), ...]. Use SerAPI-produced S-expressions and sertok outputs as machine-readable inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus preparation and train/validation/test split
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomly split corpus files into training, validation and testing sets containing 80%, 10%, 10% of the files, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train models using training and validation sets; evaluate on the held-out testing set by comparing predicted spacing to existing spacing in the test files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline metric: top-k accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate formatting predictions with top-1 and top-3 accuracy (i.e., whether the correct spacing appears in the top-k model predictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported results: Neural model top-1 99.7% / top-3 96.8%; n-gram model top-1 98.9% / top-3 93.4% (paper's reported numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about top-k accuracy (severity weighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Top-k accuracy assumes all errors are equally important, but subjective severity of spacing errors can differ greatly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies evaluation should consider severity-weighted metrics or other schemes that reflect the differing impact of spacing errors (e.g., line breaks vs minor space differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model taxonomy: n-gram baseline vs neural advanced
rubrics_metrics.description: n-gram model baseline: inserts spacing as special tokens and predicts next token by frequency after n−1 previous tokens. Neural model: embeds Coq tokens and spacing into vectors and predicts spacing using embeddings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neural model captures deeper formatting rules than statistical n-gram approach; n-gram is simpler/faster but less expressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus scale and machine-readable representation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a sizable, machine-readable corpus (e.g., MathComp-based corpus: 100k+ proof script lines, 63k+ Gallina lines, 2.2M+ Coq lexer tokens) represented as S-expressions via SerAPI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tooling requirement: use Coq + SerAPI (paper: Coq 8.10, SerAPI 0.7.1) to obtain consistent token/spacing data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration/process guideline for applying LMs to conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Workflow: 1) pick a trained language model based on preferred library/style; 2) refine the model by training on your own code; 3) use the refined model to suggest conventions in all code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule-based linters can still be useful as rerankers of LM suggestions; models should be selected/finetuned to match project/library idioms (MathComp, Stdpp, CompCert, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical formatting issues to target (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify concrete formatting problems that matter in proof scripts, e.g., unwanted line breaks before Qed, inconsistent indenting of proof scripts, and spacing differences around tokens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slides show concrete examples where neural formatting differs from manual formatting, and examples labeled as 'Problem: Line Breaks Before Qed' and 'Problem: Indenting Proof Scripts'—these are high-impact error types to prioritize in evaluation and model tuning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-based linters: pros and cons
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule-based linting is simple and fast and easy to integrate, but addresses only a small subset of conventions, is tedious to author new rules for, and cannot support all Coq languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rule-based approaches for quick checks and possibly to rerank LM suggestions, but rely on LMs to capture broader, evolving conventions across Coq variants and libraries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation protocol: compare suggested spacing against existing spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the trained model to the testing set and evaluate suggested spacing against the existing spacing in those files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the paper's basic automatic evaluation setup; consider augmenting with human judgment or severity-weighted scoring for important differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desiderata / open evaluation questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions that should guide further evaluation design: What metrics should we use to judge spacing correctness? What are the main sets of coding conventions for Coq? How can rule-based formatting be defined abstractly? Can formatting be combined with refactoring? How should formatting suggestions be integrated into Coq-based development processes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These point to required next steps: define convention taxonomies, create metrics that reflect human-perceived severity and stylistic conventions, explore combined formatting+refactoring tools, and define integration points in developer workflows (editors, CI, review).
